extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and design patent applicants/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Manual of Patent Examining Procedure guidance on evaluating design patent applications, including standards for ornamentality (35 U.S.C. 171), simulation/originality, offensive subject matter, novelty/anticipation (35 U.S.C. 102), and acceptable evidence to support or overcome rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of functional/mechanical/utility-patent information to assess ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: The functional/mechanical features of the design, the specification of an analogous utility patent (the applicant’s or another inventor), or information provided in the specification may be used to supplement the analysis of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a design is embodied in a specific mechanical article, analysis that the design lacks ornamentality because its appearance is dictated by functional requirements should be supported by reference to utility patents or other sources about the function of the design. For articles with general use, the analysis and explanation should be detailed and specific. Cite In re Carletti, 328 F.2d 1020, 140 USPQ 653 (CCPA 1964) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility during normal use is a guideline, not a statutory requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge that the article would be hidden during its end use based on examiner experience or applicant-submitted information is not prima facie evidence of functional nature; visibility during an article’s 'normal use' is not a statutory requirement of §171 but a guideline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Seiko Epson Corp. v. Nu-Kote Int’l Inc., Larson v. Classic Corp., and In re Webb to support evaluations. If evidence shows a design intended to be noticed during sale but hidden in final use, a rejection under §171 may not be necessary; but hiding during ultimate end use alone is not sufficient for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of prima facie lack-of-ornamentality rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171 for lack of ornamentality based on a proper prima facie showing fall into two categories: (A) a design visible in its ultimate end use which is primarily functional, or (B) a design not visible in its normal and intended use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support category (A) or (B) with appropriate evidence per In re Stevens, In re Webb, etc. Use form paragraphs 15.08 or 15.08.01 as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary bases that can establish prima facie lack of ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of proper evidentiary basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 that a claim is lacking in ornamentality include: (A) common knowledge in the art; (B) the appearance of the design itself; (C) the specification of a related utility patent; or (D) information provided in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections for lack of ornamentality must be supported by evidence; do not make such rejections in the absence of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shift after prima facie showing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has established a proper prima facie case of lack of ornamentality, the burden of coming forward with evidence or argument shifts to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 from the inventor or a company representative to establish intent to create the design 'for the purpose of ornamenting' (In re Oetiker; In re Carletti). Attorney arguments are not a substitute for evidence (Ex parte Webb). Use form paragraphs (e.g., 15.08) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration showing ornamentality (visible in end use)
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome a §171 rejection for an article visible in end use, an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 may be submitted from the applicant or a company representative explaining specifically and in depth which features or areas of the claimed design were created with concern for enhancing saleable value or a concern primarily for the aesthetic appearance of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Gorham Manufacturing Co. v. White and provide detailed statements of motivating factors. Attorney argument alone insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit/declaration showing ornamentality (not visible during normal use)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the design would be hidden during normal use, overcoming the rejection requires two types of evidence: (1) evidence there is some period in the commercial life where ornamentality is a matter of concern (e.g., sales literature, advertisement, catalog sheet), and (2) evidence demonstrating the design is ornamental—showing 'thought of ornament'—typically via an affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 from the applicant identifying ornamental considerations and which aspects meet them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sales literature or customer testimony for (1); for (2) identify ornamental considerations that entered into the design and which aspects meet those considerations. Examiner Notes indicate bracketed insertions (article name, evidence source).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisements and commercial materials as rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements which emphasize the ornamentality of the article embodying the claimed design may be submitted as evidence to rebut a §171 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Berry Sterling Corp. v. Pescor Plastics Inc. Provide clear, specific indication in the advertisement that the appearance is ornamental (mere inclusion in catalogs/trade shows is insufficient absent specificity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness from prior art and consumer recognition as evidence of ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the appearance of the design is ornamental may be shown by distinctness from the prior art as well as attempts to develop or maintain consumer recognition of the article embodying the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Seiko Epson Corp. v. Nu-Kote Int’l Inc. Show how claimed design differs from prior art and any branding/consumer recognition efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative designs evidence when functionality is asserted
rubrics_metrics.description: When the rejection asserts the design is purely dictated by functional considerations, evidence may be presented showing possible alternative designs which could have served the same function, indicating the claimed appearance was not purely dictated by function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite L.A. Gear Inc. v. Thom McAn Shoe Co. Provide examples of feasible alternative ornamental designs that perform same function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating a period of concern about ornamentality during commercial life
rubrics_metrics.description: When the rejection asserts no period in the commercial life of the article when its ornamentality may be a matter of concern, the applicant must establish that there is visibility at some point between manufacture/assembly and ultimate use such that ornamentality is a 'matter of concern.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Webb. Evidence can include sales materials, customer/user testimony attesting that ornamentality was of concern during selection/purchase. Inventor opinions as to purchaser reasons are insufficient to show nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of submitted evidence: look at design as a whole and influence of features
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must evaluate evidence submitted by the applicant in light of the design as a whole to decide if the claim is primarily ornamental. The determination is not based on the size or amount of the features identified as ornamental but on their influence on the overall appearance of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on overall appearance; small size of an ornamental feature does not preclude it being determinative. Use cited cases and MPEP guidance for balancing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere possibility and attempts to circumvent visibility guideline are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of encasing a concealed design element in a transparent cover simply to avoid the visibility guideline is not acceptable; applicant cannot rely on mere possibilities to provide factual evidence of ornamentality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Norco Products Inc. v. Mecca Development Inc. Applicant must provide factual evidence of ornamentality, not hypothetical workarounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that design was created 'for the purpose of ornamenting'
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171, applicant must provide evidence that he or she created the design claimed for the 'purpose of ornamenting'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Carletti. Use appropriate evidence concerning visibility and intent; mere display at trade shows/catalog inclusion is insufficient unless the material gives clear and specific indication of ornamentality (see Ex parte Webb, Berry Sterling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation/originality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 171 requires that a design be 'original.' A design which simulates an existing object or person is not original and should be rejected as lacking originality (simulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Gorham Manufacturing Co. v. White, In re Smith cases, Bennage v. Phillippi. When rejecting on simulation grounds, examiners should, if possible, provide evidence of the simulated object's appearance for comparison (use form paragraphs 15.08.02 and 15.08.03). Consider concurrent 102/103 rejections if prior art anticipates or renders obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive subject matter rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications disclosing subject matter that could be deemed offensive to any race, religion, sex, ethnic group, or nationality (e.g., caricatures or depictions) should be rejected as nonstatutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 171 and as lacking decorum/courtesy under 37 CFR 1.3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 15.09.01 and cite MPEP §608. Such disclosures are improper subject matter for design patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/anticipation standard for design patents (35 U.S.C. 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed design may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102 when anticipated (not novel) over a disclosure available as prior art; the reference 'must be identical in all material respects.' For anticipation, the ordinary observer test (the infringement test) is the sole test for anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Hupp v. Siroflex, Door-Master v. Yorktowne, Egyptian Goddess en banc, International Seaway Trading Corp. v. Walgreens. Apply the ordinary observer test considering the design as a whole and the context of prior art; small differences may be important when claim is close to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test and overall-comparison requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the ordinary observer test, if in the eye of an ordinary observer giving the attention a purchaser usually gives, two designs are substantially the same so as to deceive the observer, anticipation or infringement may be found; comparison must be of the overall design, not element-by-element isolated ornamental features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not convert the overall test into an element-by-element comparison. Account for significant differences, not trivial ones; minor differences should not prevent a finding of anticipation when designs are substantially the same (Seaway, Egyptian Goddess, Richardson, Amini, Apple v. Samsung, Ethicon v. Covidien, Sport Dimension v. Coleman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope limited to the article of manufacture recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim; it does not broadly cover a design in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re SurgiSil: ensure the claim language and figures support the article of manufacture as claimed; do not treat a design as covering other articles not recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/hidden features cannot be used to support patentability absent ornamentality showing
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102, features of the design that are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability unless the ornamentality standard under §171 is also met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Cornwall, Jones v. Progress Ind., Black & Decker v. Pittway, In re Zonenstein. If applicant wishes to rely on such features, they must meet the ornamentality evidence standard described in MPEP §1504.01(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use/public-use exceptions are limited for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental use exception to a statutory bar for public use or sale does not usually apply for design patents, although there are limited circumstances (e.g., experimentation directed to functional features) where it may negate a public use determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Mann and Tone Brothers v. Sysco. Evaluate experimental activities carefully; most experimental use defenses will not avoid a statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign design registrations, priority, and pre-AIA 102(d) use
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of a design abroad is considered equivalent to patenting for priority purposes under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and for pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) prior art purposes; U.S. design application must be made within 6 months of foreign filing to claim priority and avoid statutory bars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided country table for dates usable in 102(d) rejections; rejections under pre-AIA 102(d) should only be made when the examiner knows the foreign registration/patent actually issued before the U.S. filing date based on a foreign application filed more than six months prior. If the grant is not evident, include the specified statement in the first action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for making pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(d) as modified by 35 U.S.C. 172 should only be made when the examiner knows that the application for foreign registration/patent actually issued before the U.S. filing date based on an application filed more than six months prior to the U.S. filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the foreign grant is not evident from the U.S. record or charts, include the prescribed ¶ 15.03.01.fti statement in the first action on the merits of the application.
